rules.reason: signed-in users manage the products they created. v1 keeps the catalog owner-scoped like app-invoices; a public read rule for a storefront view is deferred (see dbbasic-package.json)
signed-in users manage the warehouse/zone/aisle/shelf/bin (and virtual customer/supplier) locations they created, same owner-scoped posture as products

signed-in users manage the stock moves they recorded. stock_moves is append-mode and immutable in spirit (see schemas/stock_moves.json) but this platform has no separate create-only permission action -- update/delete stay owner-scoped rather than granted to everyone, the same posture app-thread's append-mode thread_comments takes

signed-in users manage the backorders raised against their own catalogue, same owner-scoped posture as products. No DELETE: a customer who waited and was let down is a fact the shop should still be able to find, and `cancelled` says that out loud where a missing row would say nothing at all

a suggestion is written by system_reorder_check and ANSWERED by a human -- marked ordered when somebody bought some, dismissed when somebody looked and said no -- so read and update are the whole of what a person needs. No CREATE: a suggestion typed by hand is an observation of a shelf nobody looked at, and the nightly fold is the only thing here that has looked. No DELETE either: the pass keeps one open row per product and refreshes it, so there is nothing to tidy up, and a dismissed row is the record that somebody decided

an operator who has just set a reorder point should be able to poke the nightly pass without an admin token. It is safe to run by hand for the same reason it is safe to retry: it writes SUGGESTIONS and never a purchase order, it keeps one open row per product and refreshes rather than appends, so the worst a signed-in person can do with it is learn today's answer a few hours early
the products page is public; it shows a sign-in prompt to visitors
the locations page is public; it shows a sign-in prompt to visitors
the stock levels page is public; it shows a sign-in prompt to visitors, and computes the owner-scoped summary itself once signed in (see objects/site/stock.py)
applying a physical count is an ordinary operator verb; the object requires a signed-in identity, stamps the caller as the move's owner, and writes only compensating adjustment moves (never edits)
